papers.title: Learning Dynamics of the Influencer's Game in Resource Landscapes
papers.abstract: Across domains as varied as ecology, economics, and online platforms, individuals are incentivized to position themselves within resource-rich strategy spaces. In this work we introduce a new spatial game framework called the influencer's game. Within this new framework players' strategies are represented as positions within a trait space. Players then receive a share of a portion of a resource based on their relative influence at that resource's points traits. For the influencer's game, we show that there is a unique symmetric Nash equilibrium that exists under strict log-concavity of the influence kernel. Using the unique equilibrium we show that the stability of the system depends on the influence kernel's parameters, number of players, and the resource distribution shape. For any dimension we demonstrate a stability threshold that depends on both the scatter and curvature of the players. When this threshold is crossed, the symmetric equilibrium destabilizes and gives way to a variety of bifurcation types; including, specialist clusters, limit cycles, and sub-games that reproduce the larger game's structure. We ground these results using real-world data for resources as a demonstration of the game's application. Finally we extend the game dynamics to use multi-agent reinforcement learning and further show that the predicted bifurcation structure persists under partial observability and discretized strategy spaces. In all, the influencer's game provides a novel framework for predicting when competitive pressure drives convergence versus fragmentation with possible applications across domains.

papers.title: Influence of Assortativity on the SICP Spreading Process in Hypergraphs
papers.abstract: Many real-world systems involve group interactions that cannot be captured by pairwise graphs. They can be better represented by hypergraphs where each hyperedge could connect an arbitrary number of nodes. The Susceptible-Infected Contact Process (SICP) has been proposed to model the spreading of information and epidemics on hypergraphs. However, how higher-order topological properties of a hypergraph influence the SICP spreading process remains understudied. In this paper, we examine the impact of hypergraph assortativity based on the Neighborhood Coefficient (NC)-the average size of hyperedges incident to a node-on the SICP spreading process. By introducing a low-complexity measure of hypergraph assortativity grounded in analysis of variance, we apply hyperdegree-preserving rewirings to real-world networks and synthetic hypergraph models to tune their assortativity. We find and explain why lower NC assortativity yields higher average epidemic prevalence and lower prevalence variance across different seed selections. This phenomenon is evident when hyperdegree-preserving rewirings are applied to real-world networks with heterogeneous topological structures, but it is largely absent when comparing synthetic random hypergraphs to their rewired counterparts.

papers.title: Decisions at the end of the world
papers.abstract: International treaties are often described as tigers without teeth, failing to secure compliance or change outcomes. Cooperation also depends on how states maintain the rules they have already made -- especially where no sovereign stands above the states. Here we map more than six decades of decision-making under the Antarctic Treaty, linking submitted proposals to recorded responses and tracing how instruments act on earlier ones. Shared references tie decisions together across the agenda. Recurring revision concentrates in specialised histories, above all the management of protected areas, beyond what activity, popularity and reference age predict. Periodic administrative reviews retire outdated instruments in bulk, joining otherwise separate histories without coordinating policy across subjects. Binding Measures build overwhelmingly on earlier Measures, with little direct succession from non-binding Resolutions. Distinguishing these layers shows how a shared rule system is sustained by consensus, and provides a basis for comparing cooperation across global commons.

papers.title: Block-Fitness Modeling of the Global Air Mobility Network
papers.abstract: Accurate representations of the World Air Transportation Network (WAN) are fundamental inputs to models of global mobility, epidemic risk, and infrastructure planning. However, high-resolution, real-time data on the WAN are largely commercial and proprietary, therefore often inaccessible to the research community. Here we introduce a generative model of the WAN that treats air travel as a stochastic process within a maximum-entropy framework. The model uses airport-level passenger flows to probabilistically generate connections while preserving traffic volumes across geographic regions. The resulting reconstructed networks reproduce key structural properties of the WAN and enable simulations of dynamic spreading that closely match those obtained using the real network. Our approach provides a scalable, interpretable, and computationally efficient framework for forecasting and policy design in global mobility systems.

papers.title: Unequal Rewards and the Direction of Scientific Work: Evidence from U.S. Public Universities
papers.abstract: Research on pay dispersion has long asked whether unequal rewards increase or depress performance. Tournament theory expects stronger effort, while social comparison accounts expect withdrawal. Both perspectives, however, treat performance as a single scale on which workers can be ranked. Scientific work often resists such ordering. Some contributions extend recognized lines of inquiry and can be evaluated against prevailing standards; others revise the frames through which value is judged and become legible only later. We argue that intellectual tournaments more readily reward the first kind of contribution than the second. Pay dispersion may therefore be associated not only with how much scholars produce but also with what kinds of intellectual exploration are encouraged. We test this argument with administrative payroll records for 105,050 tenure-line faculty in 4,839 departments at 93 U.S. public universities from 2004 to 2026, linked to publication histories in OpenAlex. For each department, we estimate a separate pay equation using rank, contract basis, and seniority, then measure the Gini of the salary variation this local ladder cannot explain. Scholars in departments with greater unexplained pay dispersion publish more papers and receive more citations, but their work is less disruptive, less novel, and more conventional. Additional analyses show that compensation premiums above the ladder go disproportionately to scholars with broad collaborations and topical breadth. Although the design cannot fully separate treatment from selection, the evidence shows that inequality is not only a distributional outcome but also an evaluative structure, shaping which forms of knowledge are recognized, rewarded, and reproduced within organizations and communities.

papers.title: Collaboration drives phase transitions towards cooperation in prisoner's dilemma
papers.abstract: The emergence of cooperation among self-interested individuals is a central puzzle across biology and the social sciences. While evolutionary game theory has identified mechanisms such as spatial structure and group selection to sustain cooperation in the prisoner's dilemma, most models assume individuals revise their strategies independently. In reality, social organisms frequently form temporary coalitions to coordinate their decisions. We introduce a \emph{collaboration ring model} to investigate how such joint strategy updating affects the prisoner's dilemma. Individuals update strategies either alone---choosing a best response---or by forming coalitions where actions change only if every member is at least as well off and at least one is strictly better off. Despite individual incentives favouring defection, we show that cooperation emerges through non-equilibrium phase transitions governed by the propensity to collaborate and the benefit of cooperation. Below a critical threshold, defection dominates; above it, cooperation persists through a continuous or a discontinuous transition. Using pair approximation, we derive phase boundaries that align closely with stochastic simulations. Finally, we demonstrate that these results are robust to variations in neighbourhood and coalition size, suggesting that collaborative decision-making is a general mechanism for sustaining cooperation. Our work has potential connections to both the mutualism phenomenon in non-humans and the shared intentionality phenomenon in humans.

papers.title: Generalized Discrete Fractal Dimensions of Graph Families
papers.abstract: We study generalized discrete fractal dimensions of sequences of finite connected graphs whose diameters tend to infinity. Using normalized shortest-path metrics and a general scale function, we define regularized energy dimensions for vertex probability measures and their optimized versions. We then establish a variational principle that identifies the optimized energy dimension with the supremum of ball-mass concentration dimensions. We also establish monotonicity in the moment order, stability under uniformly comparable measures, and upper bounds in terms of R\'enyi entropy growth and the upper mass dimension. Cluster estimates and explicit graph constructions show that local vertex concentration can lower the uniform energy dimension without changing the mass dimension. Finally, for uniformly Ahlfors-regular graph families, we obtain an integral criterion for energy boundedness and explicit formulas for the critical dimensions. These results clarify how global growth, local distance distributions, and the choice of scale function jointly determine discrete fractal dimensions.

papers.title: Employment-access constraints in the 15-minute city
papers.abstract: The `15-minute city' has emerged as an influential urban-planning paradigm, promoting proximity to work and essential services. Its feasibility for journey-to-work commuting, however, has rarely been examined quantitatively. Here, we show that employment proximity is constrained by heterogeneity in the number of employees per firm. Combining urban geometry with empirically observed firm-size distributions, we derive a lower bound on commuting time that holds even under optimal workplace placement. This bound reveals a sharp transition: when employment is sufficiently unevenly distributed across firms, no spatial rearrangement of workplaces can provide uniformly short commutes. Applied to Paris and its near suburbs, with area $A=762~\mathrm{km}^2$ and empirical firm-size exponent $\hat{\gamma}\simeq 1.38$, the model predicts that only about $37\%$ of workers can reach their workplace within $15$ minutes by walking. Cycling increases this share to about $67\%$, but still leaves roughly one third of the workforce beyond the 15-minute threshold. Achieving universal short commutes would therefore require economic restructuring, differentiated mobility strategies, remote work, or a longer target time. Our results suggest replacing the universal 15-minute target, for commuting, by a city-specific benchmark determined by firm-size heterogeneity and urban scale.

papers.title: When Should Science Act on an Interstellar Anomaly?
papers.abstract: An unusual interstellar object may warrant further observation even when there is little evidence that it is artificial. The challenge is deciding which observations are worth pursuing, how much to invest in them, and when to stop. We argue that the Loeb Scale can help guide these decisions, provided its levels are understood as provisional assessments rather than estimates of the probability of extraterrestrial technology. Candidate technosignature status may justify targeted follow-up when new observations could distinguish competing explanations and the expected scientific value warrants the cost. This requires testable predictions and retrodictions, attention to natural explanations not yet considered, and recognition of the risks of false alarms. We place this argument in the broader history and philosophy of scientific anomalies and relate it to existing assessment frameworks in SETI and astrobiology. The cases of 1I/Oumuamua, 2I/Borisov, and 3I/ATLAS illustrate why classifications and research priorities must remain open to revision. Candidate status is a reason to seek better evidence while it can still be obtained, not a conclusion about an object's origin.

papers.title: Locating Debunkers for Rumor Mitigation in Directed Networks
papers.abstract: Rumors can spread widely through social networks, making the selection of a limited number of debunkers to disseminate corrective information important. Existing centrality-based methods only consider the individual influence of a node on spreading processes. Those individually influential nodes often have heavily overlapping influence ranges, resulting in a limited number of users they can cover. To address this problem, we propose the so-called Hybrid Marginal Influence (HMI) framework, which combines node centrality with additional audience coverage provided by each candidate and adaptively balances these two factors through a greedy selection procedure. We further develop the Debunker-Augmented SIR (DA-SIR) model for the propagation of rumors and corrective information. Experiments on ten real-world directed networks show that HMI generally selects debunkers with broader audience coverage than conventional centrality-based methods, accompanied by a lower final cumulative fraction of users who repost the rumor.

papers.title: Tracing dependency networks explains how origins shape downstream vulnerability
papers.abstract: Many systems sustain outcomes through chains of prerequisites, yet these dependencies are often partially observed. We trace backward from sampled outcomes to recover dependency structure and measure edge importance by the fraction of outcomes lost after an edge fails. Across 1,620 synthetic networks, revealing 90% of origins required tracing 7.24% of outcomes on average. We define pair thickness as the number of origin and outcome pairs connected through an edge. Under strict dependency, where every input is necessary, thickness counts each affected outcome once per upstream origin, whereas loss counts it once. Edges therefore form origin groups with distinct thickness and loss relations, also seen in software, citation and river topologies. Within a network, greater origin diversity corresponds to lower strict loss at equal complete thickness. We develop a growth model that predicts how edges populate these groups and how losses are distributed under partial observation, tested on 2,560 independent networks. Separating origin counts from downstream reach improves identification of edges causing the greatest losses among unsampled outcomes in strict synthetic tests. Substitutable inputs reduce losses and change which importance scores perform best. Edge importance thus measures a dependency's contribution to sustaining later outcomes, guiding the protection of critical connections.

papers.title: Inheritance of Connectivity: Modeling Higher-Order Dynamic Networks with the Birth-Death Process
papers.abstract: Higher-order networks extend pairwise interactions to represent group relationships and provide a useful framework for modeling complex systems. Understanding their dynamic evolution is important for explaining emergent structural and functional properties. However, constructing dynamic higher-order network models with stable topology remains challenging. In this paper, we propose a higher-order dynamic network model based on an inheritance-based deletion (IBAD) mechanism, which probabilistically redistributes connections when nodes or hyperedges are removed. The model combines birth-death dynamics with preferential attachment, enabling the analysis of evolving higher-order systems. Inheritance is guided by a Gaussian similarity measure based on the distance between degree histories. We derive stationary population distributions and conditional relations for connection retention and degree evolution. Simulation results show that the model generates networks with statistically stable node and hyperedge populations and heterogeneous degree distributions. The degree distributions and local clustering can be adjusted through the node and hyperedge attachment parameters. Comparisons with alternative mechanisms show that inheritance enhances connectivity relative to direct deletion, while the similarity measure influences degree heterogeneity. Comparisons with empirical networks from ecological and communication systems quantify distributional differences using Jensen-Shannon and Kullback-Leibler divergences and reveal discrepancies in clustering and within-hyperedge node-pair counts. These results provide a framework for studying population stability and structural evolution in dynamic higher-order networks.

papers.title: Scale-rich network metamaterials grow by local rules on a recursive cell division
papers.abstract: Scale-rich (SR) metamaterials are planar ligament networks grown by nucleating a segment at a random point and angle and extending it until it meets the existing structure. In the dual graph, where ligaments are nodes and junctions are links, the degree distribution has a $k^{-3}$ tail. We show that the SR construction is Cowan's iterated cell division with area-weighted selection, so the cell genealogy is a random binary search tree, and that the dual grows by a face-local rule: a new node joins two nodes on the boundary of one face. Preferential attachment on face incidences would give the Barab\'asi--Albert law, but the geometry works differently. A ligament is hit in proportion to its length, fixed at birth, and its degree is close to a Poisson variable with mean $4\ell_i(\sqrt T-\sqrt i)/c_L$, without reinforcement. Length is a fitness assigned by the cell hierarchy, $\ell_i\propto i^{-1/2}$, and the $k^{-3}$ tail follows. Integral geometry gives the probability that a new ligament cuts off a corner of its cell, which sets the triangle closure and the clustering spectrum $C(k)\simeq2p/k$. Square-closing splits raise the shortest-path multiplicity above its value at fixed degree sequence. Thickness, jamming, angle sets and density gradients leave $\gamma=3$; coherent orientation fields give $\gamma\simeq2.4$--$2.5$. For plates in three dimensions the fitness is the birth area and $\gamma=5/2$, whereas preferential attachment would give $2.44$; fluctuation tests select the fitness mechanism. The reported per-ligament energy law cannot distinguish degree from length or age.

papers.title: Persistent structural regimes in Bitcoin transactions relate to market cycles
papers.abstract: Bitcoin's blockchain is a public record of every on-chain transaction, while the price of bitcoin is set by trading on external markets. We ask whether on-chain activity alone reveals regimes associated with market trends, and whether this association remains stable over time. We summarise each week of blockchain activity from 2012 to 2026 using four measures of transaction structure and fit a two-state hidden semi-Markov model without price data. The sole market-informed constraint is an asymmetry in regime persistence, motivated by the observation that Bitcoin's price increases tend to outlast its declines. During earlier market cycles, the inferred regimes exhibit distinct transaction structures and align with periods of rising and falling prices more closely than random sequences with the same regime-duration distributions. The ongoing downturn, however, breaks this correspondence: the blockchain remains in the longer-lived regime, while its transaction structure resembles neither previous downturns nor previous upturns. Our findings support a relationship between on-chain activity and market dynamics, while highlighting its potentially time-dependent nature.

papers.title: The landscape of quantum technology companies in 2026
papers.abstract: We update our 2022 mapping of 441 quantum technology (QT) companies and examine how the industry has developed. The principal dataset now includes 1,092 companies founded with a QT focus, of which 935 remain active. Public sources and archived company websites provide evidence on company formation, technology fields and geography, alongside acquisitions, closures, valuations and involvement in artificial intelligence, defence and space. Company formation continued beyond the apparent 2018 peak in the earlier study. Computing software and applications remain the largest field, with suppliers and supporting businesses accounting for almost a third of active companies. Countries with similar company totals can have different technological profiles, and regional comparisons reveal concentrations obscured by country rankings. The first companies generally preceded the selected national policy milestones. Supporting businesses usually followed technical companies in the same jurisdiction. AI is more prevalent than defence in current company activities, while defence shows the larger increase from the earliest assessed evidence. Space relevance is documented for more than a quarter of active companies, often alongside defence involvement.

papers.title: Evolution of cooperation in multiplex interaction networks
papers.abstract: Across biological and social systems, preferential interactions among similar individuals can promote cooperation. To account for real-world interactions unfolding across multiple, simultaneous dimensions, we develop a framework for the evolution of cooperation in multiplex networks. Each layer is defined by a distinct phenotypic trait, with homophily favoring encounters between similar partners. We derive analytical conditions for natural selection to favor cooperation when phenotypes are independent or exhibit epistasis, allowing for different modes of mutation coupling. Despite payoffs being aggregated across layers, the cooperation conditions separate by layer under weak selection. Each condition depends on local payoffs and a structure coefficient determined by the effective number of phenotypes and the mutation rates. Epistasis restricts the phenotypes available on a layer and can thus shift its strategy distribution relative to that of its isolated counterpart. We show that phenotypic diversity fosters cooperation by partitioning populations into assortative niches. Furthermore, in finite populations, intensifying the prisoner's dilemma shifts the dependence of cooperation on strategy mutation from a monotonic decrease, through a U-shaped response, to a monotonic increase. Beyond weak selection, simulations show that accumulated payoffs across layers can alter mean cooperation relative to isolated systems even when phenotypes are independent. Our study unravels how homophily based on multiple phenotypes can shape the evolution of cooperation in heterogeneous populations.

papers.title: The amplifier effect of artificial agents in social contagion
papers.abstract: Individuals and organizations increasingly consider delegating decision-making to AI agents, which may significantly alter social contagion dynamics. We ask whether artificial agents exhibit different adoption thresholds from those of human subjects when making decisions and, if so, how such differences may affect the spread of social contagions. To answer these questions, we conduct two choice experiments - recently administered to human participants - with artificial agents powered by large language models (LLMs). Across two domains and five LLMs, artificial agents exhibit systematically lower adoption thresholds than human subjects. Simulations of diffusion calibrated with the experimental findings show that, holding network structure fixed, even a modest share of artificial agents leads to higher total adoption. Our findings suggest that the presence of artificial agents in social networks can alter diffusion.

papers.title: Inaccessibility in public transit networks: A study of the London and New York City subway networks
papers.abstract: The study of networks derived from infrastructure systems has received considerable attention, yet the accessibility of such systems, remains comparatively underexplored. This study examines infrastructure-based accessibility in two major legacy transit systems, the London Underground and the New York City Subway. We construct accessibility-restricted subnetworks in which nodes represent accessible stations and edges represent connections between them, and compare them with the corresponding full transit networks. We analyze the cyclomatic number, betweenness, and closeness centrality to identify key accessible hubs and differences in network organization. London has a larger share of accessible stations, and its accessible network retains more of the alternative routes of its full network, whereas New York City has a more compact accessible core concentrated around central Manhattan and major interchanges. Comparing the observed accessible stations with random sets of the same size, we find that in London they have higher betweenness centrality than random allocations, but more of their stations are beyond two stops of an accessible station, consistent with accessibility concentration at major interchanges and along fully step-free lines. In New York City, their higher betweenness centrality is fully explained by their concentration at interchanges, and their coverage is similar to that of random allocations. We also examine income and daytime activity around accessible stations. In both systems, several of the most central accessible stations are in high-activity locations, whereas accessible stations show no consistent relationship with median income. Our findings highlight substantial differences in accessibility between and within the two systems and demonstrate the utility of network-theoretic methods for understanding and improving transit infrastructure.

papers.title: Round-Based Contagion Generates Chaos from Oscillatory Dynamics: A Two-Stage Contagion Map
papers.abstract: Many social processes unfold in rounds, such as elections, meetings or turns of a game, in which individuals update synchronously. We show that this round structure can turn a regular oscillation into chaos. In Katriel's differential equations, two-stage contagion (adoption after two contacts with adopters) combined with population turnover produces bistability and relaxation oscillations, but no chaos. From the elementary reactions we derive a deterministic map $F_\tau$ for a large population updated in rounds of length $\tau$: each individual makes at most one transition per round, events compete as exponential risks, and adoptions take effect from the next round. Katriel's equations are recovered as $\tau\to0$. For short rounds the map follows the relaxation cycle, and the phase of successive outbreaks obeys a circle homeomorphism, which excludes chaos. As the rounds lengthen, this circle map loses invertibility and the invariant curve breaks down; once a round lasts about two mean adoption times, comparable to the duration of an outbreak, the attractor is chaotic, while Katriel's equations remain on a periodic relaxation cycle. With the probability $p$ of adoption after a single contact as bifurcation parameter, the map goes from extinction through a window of chaos to a stable equilibrium; for $\beta/\gamma=46$, $\mu/\gamma=0.002$, $\gamma\tau=5.5$ the window is $0.023\le p\le0.056$, bounded by the invasion threshold and by a boundary crisis, whereas Katriel's equations oscillate for $0.022<p<0.41$. Chaos is supported by the Lyapunov spectrum (Kaplan--Yorke dimension $1.81$), the correlation dimension, the 0-1 test, ordinal-pattern complexity, saddle periodic orbits and a horseshoe of the phase map. One-stage contagion, $p=0$ and permanent adoption showed no chaos.

papers.title: Modeling inhomogeneous spatial point configurations with applications to replicated patterns in real-life waiting crowds
papers.abstract: In this article, we connect statistical inference for spatial point processes with the analysis of waiting pedestrian crowds through two interconnected contributions. First, on the methodological side we develop an inference procedure for semiparametric spatial point process models leveraging replicated spatial patterns, i.e., multiple approximately independent realizations from the same process. Second, we show that spatial point processes provide a suitable modeling framework for waiting pedestrians, capturing two key aspects: spatial inhomogeneity driven by location attractiveness and repulsive interactions between pedestrians. These two components are central to the inference problem itself, since spatial point process modeling hinges on disentangling background intensity from interaction. Although replicated spatial patterns are rare in point process literature, they are available here through a unique real-life pedestrian dataset, thereby directly linking the methodological development to the physical application. We use the proposed methods to fit and evaluate determinantal and Gibbs point processes in a simulation study and a real-world case study. Despite persistent challenges in decoupling the influences of inhomogeneity from interaction, these models are able to reproduce key empirical features of waiting pedestrians.

papers.title: Glassy dynamics of metropolitan human mobility frozen near the gravitational equilibrium
papers.abstract: The doubly constrained gravity model is one of the most widely used descriptions of urban commuting flows, yet whether residential relocation can actually drive a city to this equilibrium has not been tested. We address this question by connecting urban commuting to thermal equilibrium. Using mobility data from around 30 million records across six Japanese cities over one year, we introduce the Gravity-based Origin Swapping Model (GOSM), which applies Metropolis dynamics to urban commuting by treating individuals as interacting particles. Within this framework, total commuting time defines the system energy, and temperature controls how strongly mobility responds to cost savings. Consequently, urban commuting can be analyzed through an evaluable free energy and simulated similarly to physical systems of matter, with the maximum-entropy doubly constrained gravity model serving as the stationary state. We find that the residential dynamics exhibit glassy characteristics: calibration to observed data reveals signatures of kinetically constrained models, specifically aging, hysteresis, and freezing near equilibrium. These results suggest that static OD snapshots may misestimate the effect of structural intervention: substantial improvements may require changing the urban landscape itself, through transport investment that reshapes travel times or housing development that reshapes residential capacities, rather than waiting for spontaneous relocation to reach the theoretical optimum.
